transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in today?

Most nights I end up eating a lot of food when I’m not even hungry, almost like I’m on autopilot after the day is over. It has really started to concern me, which is why I decided to come in and talk to you today.

When this happens at night, are you fully awake and aware of the eating, or do you sometimes find evidence that you ate without remembering it? Also, do you tend to eat little during the day and then feel a strong need to eat after dinner or during the night?

I am fully awake and remember everything, but I feel powerless to stop even though a part of my brain is screaming at me to put the food down. During the day, I'm so busy with work and my mom's care that I usually postpone meals or just grab something on the run, which leads to this heavy eating late in the evening when I finally sit down to plan and worry.

Do you usually eat a normal dinner and then continue eating afterward, or is most of your daily food intake delayed until the evening and night? Also, in the morning, do you often have little or no appetite for breakfast?

I definitely delay most of my eating until late in the evening, when I end up consuming a very large amount of food all at once. As for breakfast, I'm really not sure or haven't paid much attention to whether I have an appetite in the morning because I'm usually just rushing to get my day started.

On most days, do you have little or no appetite in the morning and eat more than half of your daily food after the evening meal or after waking during the night? Also, do you ever get up from sleep to eat?

No, I don't ever wake up from sleep to eat; all of this heavy eating happens late in the evening before I go to bed. In the mornings, I'm usually just too rushed and busy with my routine to eat rather than lacking an appetite entirely, though I do end up postponing most of my food until late in the day.
After these evening eating episodes, do you ever try to make up for them by vomiting, using laxatives, fasting, or exercising excessively? Also, are you very worried about your weight or shape?

No, I don't do anything like throw up, use laxatives, fast, or exercise excessively to try and make up for the food. While I feel deeply ashamed and physically uncomfortable afterward, my main distress is really about feeling completely out of control rather than being overly focused on my weight or shape.

Do these evening overeating episodes usually happen when you feel tense, anxious, or upset, and do you notice any relief in those feelings while you’re eating? Also, do they tend to occur mainly during periods of stress?

Yes, they are absolutely tied to stress and anxiety; they almost always happen when I sit down at night with my planner and start worrying about my mom's medical appointments and my work deadlines. Eating seems to give me a temporary escape and makes me feel "numbed out" from all the worry, a pattern that started about ten months ago when my mom's health first declined and my stress spiked.

During these evening episodes, do you feel a clear loss of control and eat an unusually large amount within a limited time, like a binge? Or is it more that most of your daily eating is shifted to the evening without that distinct binge feeling?

It is definitely a distinct feeling of losing control; once I start, it feels like a switch flips and I'm completely powerless to stop. I'll plow through an enormous amount of food in one sitting—like a full takeout dinner, half a loaf of bread with butter, and pantry snacks—which is way more than a normal meal. It's much more than just shifting my regular eating to the evening.

opening_question.question: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes recurrent binge-eating episodes characterized by eating an objectively large amount of food in a discrete evening period with a clear loss of control, marked distress/shame, and no compensatory behaviors. The episodes are linked to stress and have persisted for about 10 months. Night eating syndrome was considered because intake is concentrated in the evening, but the patient denies nocturnal awakenings to eat and emphasizes distinct binge episodes rather than primarily circadian delay of intake.
